readerTitle: Why the agency's warning stopped working
caseNote: 가상 사례 (마케팅 에이전시, 주택 도장 업체) + 실제 연구 (Schelling의 약속 이론) + 일화 (코르테스의 배)
insight: 위협이나 약속의 힘은 말의 세기가 아니라, 그 순간이 왔을 때 실제로 실행할 수밖에 없는 구조에서 나온다.
misconception: 더 강하게, 더 분명하게 경고하면 상대가 믿고 행동을 바꾼다.

sources.text: Schelling, T. C. (1960). The Strategy of Conflict. Harvard University Press.
에이전시와 도장 업체 사례 및 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 코르테스가 1519년 베라크루스 인근에서 배를 침몰(또는 해체)시킨 이야기는 흔히 '배를 불태웠다'로 전해지지만 세부는 과장되었을 수 있습니다. 카드에 일화임을 명시했습니다.
Schelling(1960)이 자기 선택지를 줄여 위협을 믿게 만드는 '약속(commitment)' 개념을 다뤘다는 점을 게시 전 확인하세요. 카드에는 일반적인 설명만 적었습니다.
에이전시 사례 수치(월 매출의 30%, 40일 연체)는 모두 가상 수치입니다.

cards.title: Why the agency's warning stopped working
body: A small marketing agency told its biggest client: "Pay late again and we pause all work."
The client paid 40 days late. The agency kept working. The next invoice was even later.

image.label: A stern warning email next to an unpaid invoice
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 노트북 화면에 빨간 느낌표가 달린 경고 이메일, 옆에 먼지 쌓인 미결제 청구서 더미. 청구서 위에 거미줄. 실제 회사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: How do you get paid on time?
body: You run the agency. This client is about 30% of your revenue, and they know it. Your last warning didn't change anything.
Which move is most likely to make them pay on time?

options.text: Send a firmer warning, copying their CEO
options.feedback: It raises the volume, not the stakes. The client has already seen that you keep working when they're late.

options.text: Change the contract: each month is billed upfront by card, and work starts only after payment clears
options.feedback: You give up some flexibility, but the pause now happens automatically. The client can't bet on you backing down.

options.text: Offer a 2% discount for paying within 10 days
options.feedback: It may help and keeps goodwill, but it costs you money and rewards behavior they owed you anyway.

cards.title: The client did the math.
body: The client knew that pausing work would hurt the agency more than it hurt them. Losing 30% of revenue, even for a month, could mean missing payroll.
So when the moment came, following through was the agency's worst option. The client guessed this, and they guessed right.
The warning was clear and firm. It just wasn't **believable**. Each empty warning made the next one weaker.

cards.title: Credible commitments
body: A **credible commitment** is a promise or threat that others believe because you will actually carry it out when the time comes.
The test is simple: at that future moment, will following through still be in your interest? If not, people will expect you to back down.
The economist Thomas Schelling showed a surprising fix. You can gain power by *limiting your own options*, so that backing down is no longer possible or no longer worth it.

image.label: Two paths: an open door to back down, and a locked door
image.brief: 두 갈래 길 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 "Just a warning" 길에는 "Back down" 문이 활짝 열려 있음. 오른쪽 "Commitment" 길에는 같은 문이 자물쇠로 잠겨 있음. 상대방 캐릭터가 왼쪽은 웃으며, 오른쪽은 진지하게 바라봄.

cards.title: Three ways to make your word stick.
body: Words alone rarely convince. Structure does.
list: **Remove the exit:** upfront billing, automatic shut-offs, nonrefundable terms
**Put something at stake:** a public guarantee with a penalty you must pay if you break it
**Make it automatic:** let a contract or system act, so no one has to decide in the moment
cards.callout: An old anecdote: in 1519, Hernán Cortés reportedly sank his own ships so his soldiers couldn't retreat. The story may be embellished, but the logic holds.
cards.softwareNote: "We take reliability seriously" is cheap talk. A published uptime guarantee with automatic service credits is a commitment, because breaking it costs you money without anyone choosing to pay.

cards.title: Locked doors lock you in too.
body: A commitment works because it removes your flexibility. If the situation changes, you can't easily change course. Upfront billing might push away a good client going through a short cash crunch.
It also costs something to set up: a penalty you might pay, a deal you might lose.
And if both sides lock themselves in, neither can back down. Before you commit, make sure it's a line you'd be happy to hold.

cards.title: Now it's a house-painting firm.
body: Customers often cancel the day before a job, leaving your crew idle. Your website says "late cancellations may be charged," but you've never charged anyone.
What would actually change their behavior?

options.text: Make the cancellation warning bigger and bolder on the booking form
options.feedback: It's still a threat you've never carried out. Customers who've heard about you may assume you won't.

options.text: Take a nonrefundable deposit at booking, credited toward the job
options.feedback: The cost of cancelling is already paid, so nobody has to enforce anything. You may lose a few bookers who want full flexibility.

options.text: Call every customer two days before to confirm
options.feedback: It catches some cancellations early and feels friendly. But it costs your time and gives customers no reason to stay committed.

cards.title: People believe what you'd have to do, not what you say.
body: Before making a promise or threat, ask: when the moment comes, will following through still be my best move? If not, build a structure that makes it so.
**Try it today:** find one rule your customers or partners keep ignoring. Write down one way to make it automatic.
